narration: Nigeria's new AI just cut MRI scans from twenty minutes to two minutes. Not with a new machine. With software.
visual_subject: V1 MAP-OPEN: animated Nigeria map zoom, then MRI scanner reveal

narration: The same scan that took an hour could soon take six minutes — up to ninety percent faster — on the scanners hospitals already own. And the woman behind it just won a one hundred thousand dollar national prize for it.
visual_subject: MRI suite, scanner in motion; clock/time pressure

narration: But there is one thing software like this has to prove before any hospital can trust it — and by the end of this video, you will know exactly what that is.
visual_subject: Hospital corridor, doctor walking; question hangs

narration: An MRI scan is one of the best tools in medicine — and one of the slowest. Depending on what doctors are looking for, a single scan can take fifteen minutes, thirty minutes, or an hour and a half.
visual_subject: MRI machine wide shot, patient being prepared

narration: The whole time, the patient has to lie perfectly still inside a narrow, noisy tube. For a healthy adult, that is merely unpleasant. For a child, for an elderly patient, for someone in pain or afraid of enclosed spaces, it can be impossible.
visual_subject: Patient sliding into the bore, lying still

narration: Those patients may need sedation. If they move, the scan may have to be done again. And while one patient is inside the machine, everyone else is waiting.
visual_subject: Child/elderly patient; sedation mask; patient moving

narration: It helps to know what makes this particular scan worth fighting for. An MRI does not use X-rays. It uses a powerful magnet and radio waves to look inside the body, and it can see soft tissue — the brain, the spine, organs, tumours — in a detail other scans struggle to match.
visual_subject: MRI scanner beauty shots; monitor with body images

narration: That is why, when doctors suspect a stroke, or cancer, or damage deep inside the body, this is the scan they ask for first. It is also why its slowness hurts so much. The most valuable picture in medicine is locked behind one of its longest waits.
visual_subject: Brain scan images on radiologist monitors; stroke/CT-MRI screens

narration: A faster MRI is not a luxury upgrade. It is more answers, sooner, for the patients who can least afford to wait.
visual_subject: Radiologist reading room, focused doctor at screens

narration: Nowhere is that wait heavier than in the country this invention comes from. By recent estimates, Nigeria has around zero point three MRI machines for every million people. One machine, shared by more than three million people.
visual_subject: Lagos establishing aerials; Nigeria hospital exterior

narration: When a scanner is that rare, its minutes are not just minutes — they are the difference between a diagnosis this week and a diagnosis next month. And some diagnoses cannot wait a month.
visual_subject: Crowded hospital waiting area; one scanner door

narration: A stroke cannot. A tumour cannot. Every minute a scanner spends on one patient is a minute another patient does not get.
visual_subject: Stroke emergency: ambulance, ER rush

narration: Here is the strange part. MRI machines have improved for decades. The magnets got stronger.
visual_subject: Evolution of MRI machines: older suite to modern suite

narration: The images got sharper. Computers got faster. But the scan itself never really sped up — because of how an MRI builds its picture.
visual_subject: Modern MRI suite, screens and computers close

narration: The machine does not take a photograph. It collects data, line by line, signal by signal, and only when it has collected enough of it can software assemble a clear image. More detail has always meant more data.
visual_subject: Scanner collecting data: bore lights, screen filling line by line

narration: And more data has always meant more time lying still. The entire field accepted that trade. Until someone asked whether the machine really needs all of that data — or whether some of it could be rebuilt instead.
visual_subject: Patient still inside scanner, clock; long wait

narration: That question runs into the rule everyone in medical imaging believed. You cannot skip scan data. An image rebuilt from less data would have to guess what is missing — and a guessed medical image is not a shortcut.
visual_subject: Radiologist shaking head at incomplete scan (reportage footage)

narration: It is a danger. If software invents a detail that is not there, a doctor might see a problem that does not exist. If it smooths away a detail that is there, a doctor might miss the one thing that matters.
visual_subject: Doctor studying scan detail close-up; tumour highlight on screen

narration: So the data was always collected in full, the scans stayed slow, and the queues stayed long. Breaking that rule would take more than a clever algorithm. It would take proof.
visual_subject: Full scanner sequence start-to-finish; queue outside

narration: The person who decided to try starts this story the way too many families start it. About three years ago, an elderly loved one of hers suffered a stroke. In a stroke, every second counts — how quickly a person is diagnosed can be the difference between life and death.
visual_subject: Nigerian hospital corridor; elderly patient waiting

narration: But the queues were long. His condition deteriorated while he waited. And soon after, he passed away.
visual_subject: Hospital queue; clock; empty chair

narration: She has said her vision plainly ever since: no one should suffer or die because of a delayed diagnosis. That sentence is the reason this software exists.
visual_subject: TEXT-LED over dark + Lagos hospital B-roll (quote beat)

narration: Her name is Mary-Brenda Akoda, a twenty-eight-year-old Nigerian AI research scientist. She took a First-Class degree in Computer Science from Goldsmiths, University of London, then a Master of Research with Distinction in AI and Machine Learning from Imperial College London, where she was a Google DeepMind Scholar — by her account, the only international scholar in her programme's history.
visual_subject: AKODA on camera: award/interview footage (name card pin)

narration: She worked as a software engineer and AI research scientist at Microsoft, and she has been recognised by the UK government as a global talent. The research that became this invention began in late twenty twenty-four, during her postgraduate work at Imperial.
visual_subject: Imperial College London campus; Microsoft office B-roll; London

narration: It took about a year. And when the advert for Nigeria's national science prize appeared, it was her mother — a professor of history — who sent it to her.
visual_subject: AKODA presenting / prize event footage

narration: The invention is called GenMRI, built by her company, GenScan AI. The core algorithm is known as C-MORE. Here is what it does, in plain words.
visual_subject: AKODA presentation slides/GenMRI screen if in reports; else diagram intro

narration: The scanner runs for a fraction of its usual time and collects far less data than normal. Then the AI rebuilds the full image from that smaller amount of data — using a method called a one-step consistency model.
visual_subject: DIAGRAM moment (V2-style): scanner collects LESS data, bars filling partially

narration: The critical point is where the missing detail comes from. It is anchored in the patient's own scan data — not invented from other people's pictures. Akoda herself has named the danger directly: the hardest problem was making sure the AI was not hallucinating an image that merely looked realistic.
visual_subject: MRI image assembling on screen from partial data

narration: The prize judges also noted something else: the approach could accommodate patient movement — the very thing that ruins ordinary scans.
visual_subject: Patient moving slightly in scanner; scan continues OK

narration: So what does the testing show? The system was developed on more than fifteen thousand cardiac MRI images, then validated retrospectively on more than eight thousand eight hundred MRI images — reaching up to ninety-nine point seven percent similarity to conventional scans.
visual_subject: Cardiac MRI image sequences on monitor; dataset grids

narration: Then came the test that matters more than any percentage. A consultant radiologist at Buckinghamshire Healthcare NHS Trust in the United Kingdom was shown images without being told which were conventional and which were rebuilt by the AI.
visual_subject: UK hospital (NHS) exterior + radiologist at screens, blinded test feel

narration: His verdict: the AI images were diagnostically equivalent to the conventional ones — in every case he assessed. Two peer-reviewed publications have come out of the work. If you are finding this interesting, subscribing helps this channel keep covering inventions like this one — and there is a catch coming that you need to hear.
visual_subject: Radiologist comparing two scans side by side, nodding

narration: In September twenty twenty-six, Akoda was declared the winner of the Nigeria Prize for Science and Innovation, sponsored by Nigeria LNG. The prize is twenty-two years old, and this year it drew a record two hundred and thirty-seven entries.
visual_subject: NLNG prize announcement footage; Akoda reaction/applause

narration: The judges' recommendation was unanimous. She is the first woman, and the first millennial, to win it as an individual. And here is the detail that shows what that means: the year before, the same prize looked at one hundred and twelve entries — and declared no winner at all, because none of them met the standard.
visual_subject: Award night Lagos stage; trophy/cheque moment

narration: The prize that found nobody good enough in twenty twenty-five was won, unanimously, a year later. The one hundred thousand dollar prize was presented to her in Lagos on the ninth of October.
visual_subject: Empty stage/prize graphics beat: 2025 NO WINNER (kinetic)

narration: The reaction since then explains why this story is bigger than one award. GenScan AI has received more than forty-seven letters of intent and support from healthcare providers across the United Kingdom, the United States, Kenya and Nigeria.
visual_subject: Letters/documents + hospital exteriors UK/US/Kenya/Nigeria quick cuts

narration: The company is backed by Innovate UK and works with the NHS Clinical Entrepreneur Programme. In Nigeria, the Asokoro Diagnostic and Medical Centre has agreed to support a clinical pilot — and Akoda has been clear that Nigeria should be a priority market for this technology, not an afterthought.
visual_subject: NHS building; Asokoro Diagnostic Centre Abuja if footage exists, else Abuja hospital

narration: For a country with roughly one scanner for every three million people, she is aiming the invention at home first.
visual_subject: Nigeria map with scanner dots (sparse) — graphics-led

narration: Now the honest part — because this is where inventions like this are usually oversold. GenMRI is not in hospitals today. It is pre-certification software.
visual_subject: HONEST marker over dark; tone shift

narration: The validation so far is retrospective — the AI was tested on scans that already existed — and the radiologist's assessment was an early exercise, not a full clinical trial.
visual_subject: Archive of scans on screens (retrospective feel); file/archive B-roll

narration: A similarity score of ninety-nine point seven percent is encouraging, but it is the developer's reported result, not a regulator's verdict. Nobody independent has yet watched this software perform live, on real patients, in a working hospital.
visual_subject: Regulator/office paperwork; percentage graphic small

narration: And the question from the start of this video — can an AI rebuild be trusted never to invent or erase a detail that matters — has been answered in testing, not yet in routine care.
visual_subject: Live hospital ward — patients NOT using it; empty scanner room, lights off

narration: That proof is still ahead of it.
visual_subject: Single line over dark, hold

narration: If it clears that road, the arithmetic is powerful. A scanner that finishes in two minutes instead of twenty does not just save time — it multiplies the machine. The same single scanner, in the same hospital, could see several times more patients in a day.
visual_subject: Busy MRI suite montage: back-to-back patients, fast turnover

narration: Children who today need sedation might simply lie still for two minutes. Elderly patients and people in pain would face a scan they can actually endure. Repeat scans would stop eating the day.
visual_subject: Child patient calm in scanner; elderly patient relieved

narration: And because this is software, none of it requires a hospital to buy a new machine — the scarcest, most expensive hardware in the building stays exactly where it is, and simply gets faster.
visual_subject: Same scanner, software screen updating; no new hardware

narration: What happens next is already mapped out. The company is working with clinical partners on regulatory submissions and clinical pilot programmes in the countries that have raised their hands. It has filed a US provisional patent for the technology.
visual_subject: Clinical trial/pilot footage: doctors meeting, hospital partners

narration: And it is targeting wider deployment in the second half of twenty twenty-seven. That date comes with conditions, and they matter: it depends on funding, on clinical partners, and on regulators saying yes. Akoda founded the company in January twenty twenty-six.
visual_subject: Calendar/roadmap graphics beat: H2 2027 with conditions

narration: In under two years, the work has gone from a postgraduate research project to a national prize, a blinded NHS assessment, and hospitals on four continents asking to test it.
visual_subject: AKODA recent interview footage (NTA pilots piece)

narration: So let us answer the question this video opened with. Can software really turn a twenty-minute MRI scan into a two-minute one? The honest answer is: in testing, yes — the images held up, a specialist who did not know which was which called them equivalent, and the toughest judges in Nigerian science backed it unanimously.
visual_subject: ANSWER beat: hook visuals return — map + scanner + 20→2 hero reprise

narration: In a working hospital, with a frightened child or a stroke patient on the table — that has not been proven yet. That is not a weakness in this story. It is the story.
visual_subject: Child in scanner + stroke patient ER (the stakes, plainly)

narration: One researcher lost someone to a queue, and built the thing she wished had existed. Whether it reaches the patients it was built for now depends on the slowest part of medicine — not the scan, but the proof.
visual_subject: AKODA portrait/interview closing beat; Lagos evening

narration: What do you think — if it passes its trials, would you trust a scan rebuilt by AI? Tell me in the comments.
visual_subject: Scanner running calm, end card space; comment question pin
